units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. If I only had a day. What are the five?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: First, the Grand Place. It's a paved square about sixty-eight metres by a hundred and ten, surrounded by guild houses with gilded decoration, and a Gothic town hall with a tower about ninety-six metres high.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And that's the heart.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's the heart. And what's amazing is that most of it isn't medieval.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In August of 1695, a French army under Marshal Villeroi shelled the city for two days, and most of the square was destroyed.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Only the stone shell of the town hall and a few fragments survived.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And it looks like that now?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The guilds and owners rebuilt it in about four years.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: So when you look at those golden facades, you're looking at a very fast, very proud recovery.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: UNESCO listed it in 1998.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Number two.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Manneken Pis. A small bronze boy, about fifty-five centimetres tall, relieving himself into a fountain basin on a street corner a few minutes from the Grand Place.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: People are always disappointed by how small he is.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Everyone. But he has a wardrobe of about a thousand costumes, which have their own museum nearby.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And there are two or three competing legends about why he exists, including a baby duke of Leuven who supposedly urinated on enemy troops from a basket in a tree.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Number three.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A glass-roofed shopping arcade, opened in June of 1847, designed by an architect named Jean-Pierre Cluysenaar.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's about two hundred and thirteen metres long and has three sections, the King's, the Queen's, and the Princes' galleries.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And it's still a shopping arcade.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: With chocolate shops, a theatre, a cinema, bookshops, and the Taverne du Passage.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's also where the Lumière brothers' films were shown in public in Brussels in 1896.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Four.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Boulevard Anspach and the Bourse.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Underneath that wide pedestrian boulevard, the Senne is still flowing, in a tunnel.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Between 1867 and 1871, the city buried the river because it was polluted and flooded, and built grand boulevards on top, modeled on Paris.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Bourse, the old stock exchange, was built between 1868 and 1873.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Since 2015, the boulevards around it have been mostly car-free.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And five?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Atomium. A giant steel model of an iron crystal, built for the 1958 World's Fair, which you can ride up inside for a view over the city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's out on the northern edge, so it's a metro ride away.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's more of a half-day trip, then.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is. Pick one or two of these and enjoy them, rather than rushing through all five.
